result:
Somewhere over the Pacific, it is dawn right now—and it will be dawn over some stretch of the planet at every single moment you're alive. The line between day and night sweeps westward at nearly a thousand miles an hour, dragging morning behind it like a slow parade. Fishermen in Japan greet it hours before insomniacs in Hawaii do. Nobody schedules it. It simply arrives, relentless and punctual, forever.

Light makes time travelers of us all. The warmth on your face left the sun eight minutes ago; you're constantly touched by the recent past. On a dark night, the situation turns vertiginous. Andromeda, that faint oval smudge above us every autumn, sends light that departed before our species existed. Early humans were learning stone tools when those photons started their commute.

Betelgeuse, the ruddy shoulder of Orion, could blow tomorrow—or may have blown centuries ago, its farewell still crossing the void. One night we'll look up and the familiar constellation will hold something new, a point of light bright enough to read by at midnight.

We act as though "now" were universal, but physics won't vouch for it. Everything arrives late: light to your eyes, sound to your ears, nerve signals crawling far slower than electricity. Consciousness trails reality by a fraction of a second.

So we are all watching reruns—a little delayed, a little dated, forever catching up. Personally, I find that comforting rather than sad. Being late to the universe beats missing it entirely.

Somewhere over the Pacific, it is dawn right now—and it will be dawn over some stretch of the planet at every single moment you're alive. The line between day and night sweeps westward at nearly a thousand miles an hour, dragging morning behind it like a slow parade. Fishermen in Japan greet it hours before insomniacs in Hawaii do. Nobody schedules it. It simply arrives, relentless and punctual, forever.

Light makes time travelers of us all. The warmth on your face left the sun eight minutes ago; you're constantly touched by the recent past. On a dark night, the situation turns vertiginous. Andromeda, that faint oval smudge above us every autumn, sends light that departed before our species existed. Early humans were learning stone tools when those photons started their commute.

Betelgeuse, the ruddy shoulder of Orion, could blow tomorrow—or may have blown centuries ago, its farewell still crossing the void. One night we'll look up and the familiar constellation will hold something new, a point of light bright enough to read by at midnight.

We act as though "now" were universal, but physics won't vouch for it. Everything arrives late: light to your eyes, sound to your ears, nerve signals crawling far slower than electricity. Consciousness trails reality by a fraction of a second.

So we are all watching reruns—a little delayed, a little dated, forever catching up. Personally, I find that comforting rather than sad. Being late to the universe beats missing it entirely.
